title: Book 9 — Calliope, Chapter 71
paragraphs: Among the barbarians, those who proved themselves the best men were, of the foot, the Persians, and of the cavalry, the Sacans; and for a single man, Mardonius, it is said, was the best. Of the Greeks, though both Tegeans and Athenians proved themselves good men, the Lacedaemonians surpassed them in valor. Of this I have no other proof (for all these were victorious over their opposite numbers), except this: that they fought the strongest part of the enemy's force and overcame it. The man who, in my opinion, by far proved himself the best was that Aristodemos who, having come back alone of the three hundred safely from Thermopylae, had reproach and dishonor attached to him. After him the best were Poseidonios, Philokyon, and Amompharetos the Spartan. However, when there was discussion of which of them had shown himself the best, the Spartans present gave it as their opinion that Aristodemos had evidently wished to be killed, because of the charge against him, and so, as if in a frenzy and leaving his place in ranks, had performed great deeds, whereas Poseidonios had proved himself a good man although he had not wanted to be killed — and to that extent he was the better of the two. This, however, they perhaps said out of ill will. All those I named of the men killed in this battle were especially honored, except Aristodemos; but Aristodemos, because he had wanted to be killed on account of the aforementioned charge, was not honored.
